meeting_text.who: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand (“the RBNZ”, often called “the Reserve Bank”), New Zealand’s central bank. Its interest rate decisions are made by the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), chaired by Governor Anna Breman. The MPC tries to agree as a group (by “consensus”). When it cannot, it votes, and since May 2026 each member’s vote is published by name. From October 15 the Committee gains a seventh member, Rebecca Williams.
meeting_text.meeting: October 2026 Monetary Policy Review (a shorter decision without a full new forecast; the full forecast document, the Monetary Policy Statement, comes four times a year)
meeting_text.decision: Wednesday, Oct 28, 2:00 p.m. New Zealand time (NZDT). That is 01:00 UTC on Oct 28, or 9:00 p.m. U.S. Eastern Time on Tuesday, Oct 27. A media conference follows from the RBNZ’s Auckland office.
meeting_text.after: Wednesday, December 9, 2026 (Monetary Policy Statement, with new forecasts)

why_steps.title: The RBNZ has one main job, and one main tool
why_steps.html: The Reserve Bank’s main job is to keep prices steady. Its target is that prices should rise between 1% and 3% a year, aiming for the 2% midpoint over the medium term. It also tries to avoid unnecessary swings in jobs and output, so it watches unemployment closely. Its main tool is the Official Cash Rate, or OCR. In the RBNZ’s words, it is “the interest rate that banks earn on their deposits with us”, and it also sets what banks pay when they borrow from the Reserve Bank. That flows through to floating mortgages, business loans and savings accounts. Think of it like the pedals of a car. Raising the OCR is pressing the brake: loans get more expensive, so people and companies borrow and spend less, and prices cool down. Cutting is pressing the gas. Holding means keeping your foot where it is. Today the OCR is 2.75%. In July the RBNZ described the rate as still “accommodative”, meaning it is still giving the economy a little gas (July record).

why_steps.title: Prices are above the band, and mostly because of fuel
why_steps.html: Consumer prices (the CPI, or consumers price index, from Stats NZ) were 4.1% higher in the June 2026 quarter than a year earlier, up from 3.1% in March (Stats NZ). In simple terms: a basket of everyday things that cost NZ$100 a year ago now costs about NZ$104.10. The goal would be about NZ$102. Unlike most countries, New Zealand measures the CPI only once every three months, so each report is a big event. Look underneath. Without petrol and diesel, prices rose 2.9%. Prices of imported and traded goods rose 4.9%, but only 2.1% without fuel. In August, petrol was up 17.9% and diesel 45.8% on a year earlier (Treasury). The worry is the home-grown part: prices of things that cannot be imported, like rent, insurance and services (“non-tradables”), are rising 3.4%, and the average of the RBNZ’s “core” measures, which strip out jumpy prices, rose from 2.4% to 2.7% (RBNZ September MPS). One example of a core measure is a trimmed mean: drop the biggest price rises and falls each quarter and average the rest.

why_steps.title: So the RBNZ has pressed the brake twice
why_steps.html: After cutting the OCR to 2.25% in late 2025, the RBNZ held through May. In May the Committee split 3–3, and Governor Breman’s casting vote kept the rate on hold (RBNZ). It then raised to 2.50% on July 8 and to 2.75% on September 2, both times by consensus. In September it said: “Conditional on the central economic outlook, members judged that the OCR may need to increase further.” Its own projection has the OCR rising to about 3.2% over the next two years, which implies roughly two more 0.25-point rises (RBNZ). The mood inside the Committee has also shifted. In July, two of six members saw the risks to inflation as tilted upward. By September it was four of six (Gourley, Silk, Gai and Governor Breman), with Conway and Hansen seeing risks as balanced.

why_steps.title: Reasons the RBNZ might raise again in October
why_steps.html:
• Oil is far above what the RBNZ assumed. Its September forecasts assumed Dubai oil of about US$85 a barrel for the September quarter. Brent oil hit US$135.51 on October 2 and was US$125.44 on October 6 (FRED). Governor Breman said on September 22: “If higher oil prices persist, they are expected to result in somewhat higher near-term inflation” (RBNZ).
  • The Kiwi dollar is weaker than assumed. The RBNZ assumed a trade-weighted index of 66.9. On October 14 it was 63.94, and one NZ dollar bought only US$0.562 (RBNZ). A weaker currency makes imported fuel and goods dearer.
  • Markets expect it. In mid-September, Treasury said markets priced about a 70% chance of an October rise (Treasury). The 90-day bank bill rate (3.23%) is well above the OCR, consistent with that.
  • The Committee’s balance has tilted. Four of six members saw upside inflation risk in September. Chief Economist Paul Conway warned that “businesses pass on cost increases more readily now than in the past” (speech).
  • Other central banks are braking. The U.S. Fed raised to 3.75%–4.00% and the ECB’s deposit rate is 2.50% after a September rise.

why_steps.title: Reasons the RBNZ might wait until December
why_steps.html:
• The economy is weak. GDP grew only 0.2% in the June quarter and household spending was flat (Stats NZ). Unemployment is 5.6%, and the RBNZ expects it to stay above 5% until 2028.
  • Fuel has not clearly spread. Food inflation slowed to 1.9% in August and rents were flat (Treasury). Pay is rising only 2.0%–2.8% a year. Treasury found “little evidence so far of spillover into wider domestic and non-fuel prices.”
  • Markets already pressed the brake. The 10-year government bond rate rose from a 4.46% June average to about 5% (4.98% on October 13). Fixed mortgage rates follow these wholesale rates.
  • December brings full forecasts. October is a shorter Review. December’s Statement will have new forecasts, the September quarter jobs report and another quarter of inflation-expectations surveys.
  • “May”, not “will”. September’s wording (“may need to increase further”) was softer than July’s (“further OCR increases appear likely”).

why_steps.title: Weighing both sides

left: Oil far above the RBNZ’s assumption
4 of 6 members saw upside inflation risk
right: Food and rents cooling, slow pay growth

why_steps.html: Both sides are strong. What tips us slightly toward Raise is that the main new information since September (oil and the currency) points the same way as the Committee’s own worries, and markets were already expecting a move. The RBNZ also tends not to like surprising markets. That is why we say about 55% Raise, 42% Hold and 3% Cut, not something more lopsided.

why_steps.title: The one thing to watch: September quarter prices
why_steps.html: Before the meeting, Stats NZ publishes the CPI for July–September (we could not confirm the exact date on its calendar). The RBNZ forecast annual inflation of 3.9% for that quarter (MPS). If inflation comes in at 4.2% or more, or non-tradables inflation stays at 3.4% or higher, we would move to about 70% Raise. If it comes in at 3.7% or less with non-tradables easing, Hold would become our main call. Monthly price data on October 16 (petrol, food, rents) will give an early hint.

verdict.headline: RAISE
verdict.sub: Raise the interest rate by 0.25 points, from 2.75% to 3.00%. This is a close call. A pause (Hold) is a very real possibility.
verdict.confidence_note: “Low” means this is not far from a coin flip. The September quarter consumer price report, due from Stats NZ before the meeting (we could not confirm the exact date), could be enough to change our answer. No decision was made in early October: the last one was on September 2.
verdict.short_version: New Zealand prices are rising 4.1% a year, above the 1%–3% target band, mostly because of fuel. The RBNZ has already raised its rate twice (July and September) and said it “may need to increase further”. Since then oil has jumped again and the Kiwi dollar has weakened, both of which push prices up. But the economy is weak and unemployment is 5.6%. We think the RBNZ will more likely press the brake once more in October than wait until December, but it is close.

why_title: Why we think this, step by step
story_intro: This is the story of the past year, in order. Each step explains what happened, why it happened, and what it meant for ordinary people. The line at the bottom of each step (“Because of this…”) shows how it led to the next step, so you can follow cause and effect from start to finish.

timeline.title: The RBNZ cut the OCR three times, to 2.25%
timeline.what: The OCR went from 3.25% to 3.00% in August, to 2.50% in October (a big 0.50-point cut) and to 2.25% in November. The November cut was decided by a 5–1 vote; the RBNZ did not name the dissenter.
timeline.why: The economy had shrunk in the June 2025 quarter by more than expected, and there was lots of spare capacity. In October the Committee weighed 0.25 against 0.50 and chose the bigger cut. Inflation was around the top of the band (3.0% in the September 2025 quarter), but expected to fall back to 2%.
timeline.people: Floating mortgage rates and business loans got cheaper. Term deposits paid less.
timeline.because: with the OCR well below “neutral”, the RBNZ stopped to let the cuts work.

timeline.title: A new Governor, a pause at 2.25%
timeline.what: At her first Monetary Policy Statement as chair, Governor Anna Breman’s Committee held the OCR. It noted “Annual consumers price inflation increased to 3.1 percent in the December 2025 quarter” and “the unemployment rate increased to 5.4 percent”. It said: “If the economy evolves as expected, monetary policy is likely to remain accommodative for some time.”
timeline.why: Growth had bounced back (GDP +1.1% in the September 2025 quarter), and inflation was expected to fall toward 2% within a year. There was no reason to press either pedal.
timeline.people: Borrowing costs stayed low. Most talk was about when, much later, rates might start to rise.
timeline.because: the RBNZ was sitting still with its foot near the gas when a new shock arrived from the Middle East.

timeline.title: The Middle East conflict: an oil shock
timeline.what: Conflict in the Middle East “significantly reduced the supply of oil, gas and other petrochemicals” through the Strait of Hormuz. On April 8 the RBNZ held at 2.25% (by consensus), forecast inflation of 4.2% for the June quarter, and warned that if fuel started pushing up other prices, “decisive and timely increases in the OCR would be required.”
timeline.why: New Zealand imports all of its fuel. Dearer oil means dearer petrol, diesel, freight and flights, which feed into many prices. But it also squeezes household budgets, which slows the economy.
timeline.people: Filling the car got much more expensive within weeks. The RBNZ noted households were already facing “weak real income growth, high unemployment and house price weakness.”
timeline.because: the question became: will the RBNZ “look through” the fuel jump, or brake to stop it spreading?

timeline.title: A 3–3 split, settled by the Governor
timeline.what: The Committee split evenly. Breman, Silk and Conway voted to hold at 2.25%; Hansen, Gourley and Gai voted to raise to 2.50%. The Governor’s casting vote kept the rate on hold. The RBNZ said “the OCR will most likely need to increase sooner and by more than envisaged” and that it expected rises “this year”. March quarter inflation was 3.1%.
timeline.why: Half the Committee wanted to act early against inflation; the other half worried more about weak growth (2026 growth was cut by 0.9 points).
timeline.people: For the first time, New Zealanders could see each member’s vote, thanks to new transparency rules from April 30. Markets started preparing for rises.
timeline.because: a rise at the next meeting looked very likely.

timeline.title: First rise: the OCR goes to 2.50%
timeline.what: The RBNZ raised by 0.25 points, by consensus. Oil had dropped after “the partial reopening of the Strait of Hormuz”, but the RBNZ said the effects “will linger for some time”. It added: “while further OCR increases appear likely at upcoming meetings, their timing is highly uncertain.”
timeline.why: Inflation was expected to peak at 3.9% in the June quarter and stay above the band for several quarters. The Committee judged the OCR was still “accommodative”, giving the economy gas it no longer needed.
timeline.people: Floating mortgage rates rose a little. Savers started to earn slightly more.
timeline.because: everyone waited for the June quarter price and job numbers.

timeline.title: Inflation 4.1%, unemployment 5.6%
timeline.what: CPI inflation came in at 4.1%, above the RBNZ’s July estimate of 3.9%. Without fuel it was 2.9%. Unemployment rose to 5.6%. Wage rates rose only 2.0% a year.
timeline.people: A household whose costs were NZ$1,000 a week a year ago now paid about NZ$1,041, while pay rose only about NZ$20 per NZ$1,000.
timeline.because: the RBNZ judged that inflation was the bigger danger.

timeline.title: Second rise: the OCR goes to 2.75%
timeline.what: In its September Monetary Policy Statement the RBNZ raised by 0.25 points, by consensus: “Inflation increased to 4.1 percent in the June quarter because of higher fuel prices arising from the conflict in the Middle East.” It said the OCR “may need to increase further”, forecast 3.9% inflation for the September quarter, and projected the OCR rising to about 3.2%.
timeline.people: Mortgage rates for 6-month to 2-year terms had already risen 0.20–0.30 points since May, and the Kiwi dollar rose a little as investors expected more rises.
timeline.because: markets began pricing another rise for October.

timeline.title: A weak economy, and markets expect more
timeline.what: GDP grew only 0.2% in the June quarter, with household spending flat. Treasury said markets priced about a 70% chance of an October rise. On September 29 Treasury’s pre-election update said “An emerging economic recovery has been delayed by higher oil prices.”
timeline.people: House prices were 0.9% lower than a year earlier in August, and house sales were down 13%. Many people felt poorer.
timeline.because: the October call hinged on whether new shocks pushed inflation risk up further. They did.

timeline.title: Oil spikes again, the Kiwi dollar slides
timeline.what: Brent oil rose from US$115.91 on September 30 to US$135.51 on October 2, then eased to US$125.44 on October 6. One NZ dollar fell from about US$0.58 in mid-September to US$0.56. The New Zealand 10-year bond rate hit about 5.1% in late September. Governor Breman said: “Recent increases in global oil prices and longer-term interest rates reflect the challenging environment we face.”
timeline.people: Fuel prices at the pump are likely to stay high, and imported goods dearer. Fixed mortgage rates face upward pressure from higher bond rates.
timeline.because: the case for a third rise strengthened just as the RBNZ entered the run-up to October.

timeline.title: Setting the stage for October 28
timeline.what: The RBNZ confirmed the October Review will be published on October 28 at 2 p.m., with a media conference in Auckland. Rebecca Williams joins the Committee on October 15. The OCR is 2.75%, the 2-year government bond rate 3.80%, the 10-year 4.98%, and the trade-weighted index 63.94. A general election follows on November 7.
timeline.because: our reading is “raise again, unless September prices surprise on the low side”, which is why our main call is Raise, with Hold close behind.

choices_intro: At every meeting the RBNZ has three options. Below we explain what each one would mean, why it could happen, why it might not, and what it would mean in everyday life. Analysis · our judgement

choices.title: Raise: up 0.25 points, to 3.00%
choices.meaning: the RBNZ presses the brake for the third meeting in a row, to stop the fuel shock from turning into lasting inflation. It would likely keep saying further moves depend on the data.
for: Oil is much higher than planned. Brent was US$125.44 on October 6, against an RBNZ assumption of about US$85 (Dubai) for the September quarter.
The Kiwi dollar is weaker. The trade-weighted index is 63.94, versus the 66.9 the RBNZ assumed. Imports cost more.
The Committee leans hawkish. Four of six members saw upside inflation risk in September, and the RBNZ’s own track points to about 3.2%.
Markets expect it. About 70% priced in mid-September (Treasury); the 90-day bank bill rate is 3.23%, almost half a point above the OCR.
Inflation is far above target. 4.1% in the June quarter, with non-tradables at 3.4% and core measures rising.
against: The economy is fragile. GDP +0.2%, household spending flat, unemployment 5.6%.
Spillover is limited so far. Food inflation 1.9%, rents flat, pay growth 2.0%–2.8%.
A soft September CPI could persuade the Committee to wait for December’s full forecasts.
choices.everyday: floating mortgage rates and overdrafts would rise by roughly a quarter point within weeks. On a NZ$500,000 floating mortgage, that is about NZ$1,250 more interest a year (our rough calculation). Term deposits would pay a bit more, and the Kiwi dollar might firm up.

choices.title: Hold: keep the OCR at 2.75%
choices.meaning: the RBNZ keeps its foot where it is for now, while signalling that more rises are likely. It would be a “not yet”, not a “we are done”.
for: Weak growth and high unemployment. Braking harder could push unemployment above 6%.
Bond markets did some of the work. The 10-year rate rose from a 4.46% June average to about 5%. That makes fixed mortgages and business loans dearer.
December is a better moment. The December Statement brings full new forecasts and the September quarter jobs data.
Softer wording. September’s “may need to increase further” is less firm than July’s “appear likely”.
Two rises are still working through. It takes many months for a rate change to have its full effect.
against: Oil and the currency moved the wrong way since the September forecasts.
Surprising markets is costly. With a rise largely expected, a hold could push the Kiwi dollar down further, adding to imported inflation.
A hot September CPI would make waiting look risky.
choices.everyday: floating loan and savings rates would stay about where they are for now. Fixed mortgage rates would keep following wholesale rates, which already expect rises.

choices.title: Cut: lower the OCR
choices.meaning: the RBNZ would switch from the brake to the gas, reversing two recent rises.
for: Only in an emergency: for example a financial crisis, a sudden collapse in oil prices with a global downturn, or a sharp jump in layoffs before October 28.
Even then, the RBNZ would more likely hold first than cut straight away.
against: Inflation is 4.1%. Cutting would add fuel to rising prices.
Nobody is asking for it. In the statements and speeches we read since July, no MPC member argued for a cut.
The RBNZ’s own track points up, to about 3.2%.
choices.everyday: loans would get slightly cheaper, but the surprise itself would signal that something had gone badly wrong in the economy.

change.lead: Our 55% / 42% / 3% guess is based on what we know today. New information arrives almost every day. Some of it can move our view a lot. Here is what we are watching, and why each item matters.
change.intro: The RBNZ can only react to information it has already seen. A report released before October 28 can change the October decision. A report released after it can only shape what happens on December 9. That is why the reports in the first part of the table matter most right now. Note that New Zealand is many hours ahead of Europe and America: the RBNZ decides before the U.S. Fed, which announces later the same calendar day in Washington.

decision_row.name: OCR decision · Monetary Policy Review
decision_row.what: The answer, with a summary record of the meeting and a media conference.

table.name: New MPC member starts (Rebecca Williams)
table.what: The Committee grows from six to seven members.
table.why: An odd number makes a tied vote less likely. Her views on policy are not yet public.
table.trigger: Any public comments from her would be read closely. Small effect on its own.

table.name: Selected price indexes, September
table.what: Monthly prices for food, rents, petrol, power and some other items.
table.why: The first look at September prices, and a preview of the quarterly CPI.
table.trigger: Petrol up sharply again and rents rising → leans Raise. Food and rents still flat → small push toward Hold.

table.name: Electronic card transactions, September
table.what: How much people spent using debit and credit cards.
table.why: Shows whether households are still cutting back.
table.trigger: A strong rise → small push toward Raise. A fall → leans Hold.

table.name: BNZ-BusinessNZ manufacturing survey (PMI), September
table.what: Whether factories are expanding (above 50) or shrinking (below 50).
table.why: An early sign of whether the recovery Breman expects is happening.

table.name: Consumers price index (CPI), September quarter
table.what: How much the prices families pay changed from July to September, including non-tradables.
table.why: The single most important report before the meeting. The RBNZ forecast 3.9% annual inflation.
table.trigger: Annual CPI 4.2% or more, or non-tradables 3.4% or higher → Raise about 70%. CPI 3.7% or less with non-tradables easing → Hold becomes our top pick.

table.name: Kiwi dollar
table.what: The value of the NZ dollar and the price of crude oil.
table.why: The two biggest changes since the September forecasts.
table.trigger: Brent back below US$100 and the TWI back above 66 → leans Hold. Brent above US$130 → leans Raise.

table.name: Voting opens for the general election
table.what: New Zealanders can start voting; election day is November 7.
table.why: The RBNZ sets the OCR independently of politics, so we do not expect the election to change its decision.

table.name: OCR decision · Monetary Policy Review
table.what: The answer, with a summary record of the meeting and a media conference.

table.name: U.S. Federal Reserve decision
table.what: The U.S. rate decision (2:00 p.m. on Oct 28 in Washington).
table.why: Too late for October. A U.S. rise could weaken the Kiwi dollar further.

table.name: Labour market statistics, September quarter
table.why: Will show whether the job market is turning up, as filled-jobs data suggest.

table.name: General election day
table.what: New Zealand chooses its next government.
table.why: Could change government spending plans, which affect demand and inflation over time.

table.name: Financial Stability Report
table.what: The RBNZ’s check on the health of banks, borrowers and the financial system.
table.why: Shows how households are coping with higher rates.

table.name: OCR decision · Monetary Policy Statement
table.what: The next decision, with full new forecasts.
table.why: If October is a hold, December is when we would expect the next rise.

change.caption: Upcoming reports and events (New Zealand time)
change.other_title: Other things that could move our view
other: Oil and the Middle East. Fuel is the main driver of today’s inflation. Brent jumped to US$135.51 on October 2 before easing to US$125.44 on October 6 (FRED). A sustained move back below US$100 would make waiting much easier. Another spike would make a rise more likely, and could even put a 0.50-point rise on the table.
The Kiwi dollar. A further slide (for example below US$0.55) would add to imported inflation and push toward Raise.

Final words from the RBNZ. The last on-the-record comments we found are Governor Breman’s from September 22. Any speech or interview before October 28 is a direct hint. Central banks usually avoid policy comments in the days just before a decision.

Bond markets. If the 10-year rate falls back sharply, one argument for Hold (that markets already tightened) weakens. If it rises well above 5%, the RBNZ may feel the market is doing more of the work.
A financial shock. A sudden market fall or trouble at a bank would almost certainly push the RBNZ to hold.

report_intro: Think of this as a school report for the economy in four subjects. Green means healthy. Yellow means mixed, keep watching. Red means a problem the central bank must fix. Each grade is also written in words, so you do not need to see the color. Analysis

report_card.one: Prices are 4.1% higher than a year ago, above the 1%–3% band.
report_card.look: Consumer prices (CPI, up 4.1%), CPI without fuel (2.9%), the RBNZ’s core measures (average 2.7%), non-tradables (3.4%), and inflation expectations (2.3% two years ahead).
report_card.why: Headline inflation is well above the band and the RBNZ expects it to stay above for several quarters. Home-grown (non-tradables) inflation is 3.4%, and core measures rose. Oil has jumped again and the Kiwi dollar is weaker than assumed. Some comfort: expectations are near 2%, food inflation is under 2%, and rents were flat in August.
report_card.change: Oil falling back, and non-tradables inflation easing toward 3% or below.
report_card.matters: This is the main reason the RBNZ is raising rates at all. As long as this stays red, it leans toward pressing the brake.

report_card.one: Unemployment is high at 5.6%, but hiring is slowly picking up.
report_card.look: The quarterly unemployment rate, monthly filled jobs, job ads, and wage growth.
report_card.why: Bad news: unemployment rose to 5.6%, and the RBNZ says job growth has not been enough to absorb new workers. Real pay is falling. Better news: employment rose 0.4% in the June quarter, filled jobs are up 0.9% on a year ago (August), and job ads are up 9.7%. Not bad enough to be red, not healthy enough to be green.
report_card.change: Unemployment rising toward 6% → red. Unemployment falling and job ads rising further → green.
report_card.matters: This is the main reason the RBNZ might wait. Slow wage growth also means wages are not driving inflation.

report_card.one: Exporters are doing well, but households are holding back.
report_card.look: GDP (the total value of everything the country produces), household spending, retail sales, exports, business confidence and house prices.
report_card.why: GDP rose only 0.2% in the June quarter (1.7% on a year ago) and household spending was flat. Retail volumes fell 0.5%. House prices are slipping. On the other side, goods exports were up 15% in August from a year earlier, and business confidence is high (ANZ +51.9). The RBNZ expects growth of 0.5% in the September quarter.
report_card.change: Clear signs of a household spending pick-up → green. Falling business confidence or a weak September quarter → red.
report_card.matters: A weak economy makes each rate rise more painful. The RBNZ estimates spare capacity (an “output gap”) of about −1.5% of GDP, which should slowly pull inflation down.

report_card.one: Borrowing costs have jumped, and the Kiwi dollar is weak.
report_card.look: Wholesale interest rates (90-day bank bills, 2-year and 10-year government bonds), and the NZ dollar.
report_card.why: Worrying: the 10-year government bond rate rose from a 4.46% June average to about 5% (4.98% on October 13). The NZ dollar fell to about US$0.56, and the trade-weighted index (63.94) is well below the RBNZ’s 66.9 assumption. Reassuring: markets are orderly, and the 2-year rate (3.80%) shows investors trust the RBNZ to keep raising if needed.
report_card.change: A further slide in the currency or a disorderly jump in bond rates → red. A calmer currency and lower long rates → green.
report_card.matters: Higher market rates already cool borrowing, which helps the case for waiting. A weak currency pushes the other way.

gaps_intro: Good research is honest about its blind spots. Here is what is missing, delayed or unverified, and why it matters.
gaps: The exact date of the September quarter CPI. Stats NZ’s release calendar could not be read by our tools, so we list it as “late October, before the decision”. Why it matters: it is the most important report before the meeting, and our view may change the day it comes out.

Up-to-date market odds for October. The only figure we found is Treasury’s mid-September reading of about 70%, before the latest oil spike. We did not collect overnight index swap pricing. Why it matters: we cannot compare our 55% chance of a rise with what markets expect today.

Full Stats NZ releases. For the June quarter CPI, labour market, GDP and other releases we could read only the headline summary on Stats NZ’s pages; further details (such as non-tradables inflation, wage growth and household spending) come from the RBNZ’s September Statement and Treasury’s summaries, and exact release days were not collected. Why it matters: small details could differ from the full official tables.

Individual core inflation measures and household inflation expectations (trimmed mean, weighted median, sectoral factor model; household surveys) were not collected; we have only the RBNZ’s average and description.

Recent speeches. We found no MPC speech between Governor Breman’s September 22 Dunedin remarks and today, and did not read the September media-conference transcript. Why it matters: late hints often shape the decision.

Who votes in October. We assume seven members (with Rebecca Williams joining and Karen Silk staying until December), but the RBNZ has not confirmed attendance. We also do not know the November 2025 dissenter’s identity.
Mortgage rates, building consents, card spending for September, the Quarterly Survey of Business Opinion and dairy prices were not collected.
Oil figures differ by source. Treasury quoted WTI at US$89.4 on September 29, while FRED shows US$97.18 on September 30. We used FRED. We did not collect the Dubai price the RBNZ uses.
The RBNZ’s neutral OCR estimate and the full September projection tables were not in the parts of the Statement we could read.

How we gathered data: the data were gathered with web search and direct page reads on Oct 14, 2026. The search engine itself was blocked in our tools, so every number was read directly from the official or named page linked next to it (RBNZ, Stats NZ, NZ Treasury, the Electoral Commission and FRED).
numbers_intro: Every number we used, grouped by topic. For each one you will see the latest value, the period it covers, when it was published, the previous value, where it came from, and, most importantly, a plain explanation of what it is and why it matters. Tap a group to open or close it. Observed facts

live_before.html: The numbers on this page are a snapshot taken on October 14, 2026. If you want to see whether anything has changed since then, you can try loading the newest values from FRED, a free public data service run by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Note: FRED does not carry an up-to-date New Zealand CPI series (its OECD copy stops in early 2025), so for prices use Stats NZ and the RBNZ directly. Several New Zealand series on FRED are monthly or quarterly OECD copies that arrive months late, and its unemployment copy (5.3% for the March quarter) differs slightly from Stats NZ’s published 5.4%. For daily interest and exchange rates, the RBNZ’s own statistics pages are more current.

How it works: FRED gives anyone a free “API key”, a code that works like a library card for its data. Paste your key below and press Refresh. The newest values appear in a separate table, next to our snapshot values so you can compare. The rest of this page stays exactly as it is.
Privacy: your key is saved only in this browser, on this device, and is sent only to FRED. Press “Forget key” to remove it. Get a free key at fred.stlouisfed.org.

live_after.html: Good to know: FRED often does not allow web pages to request its data directly, so many browsers will block this. If that happens, you will see a clear message and nothing on the page will change. You can always check the same numbers yourself on the FRED website.

overview.last_move: Raised 0.25 pts on Sep 2, 2026 (second rise in a row)
overview.card_why: Oil and a weaker Kiwi push inflation (4.1%) further above target; a fragile economy keeps a pause close behind.

overview_paragraph: The same energy shock is pushing prices up almost everywhere, and five of the eight banks (the Fed, BoJ, ECB, RBNZ and RBA) have already raised rates this year. Our main call is a pause at seven of the eight meetings and a rise in New Zealand, but the chance of a rise is real nearly everywhere: highest in New Zealand, Australia, the UK, the U.S. and the euro area. Switzerland, with inflation of just 1%, is the exception.

G.name: Prices
G.intro: These numbers tell us how fast things are getting more expensive in New Zealand. The RBNZ’s job is to keep yearly inflation between 1% and 3%, aiming for the 2% midpoint over the medium term. New Zealand measures consumer prices only once every three months (quarterly), so each CPI report carries a lot of weight.

w: What it is: Stats NZ checks the prices of hundreds of everyday things, like food, rent, petrol and power, every three months, and compares them with a year earlier. A 4.1% rise means a basket that cost NZ$100 a year ago now costs about NZ$104.10.

Why it matters: this is the number the RBNZ’s 1%–3% target is based on. At 4.1% it is well above the top of the band, mainly because of fuel. The September quarter figure is due before the October 28 decision (exact date not confirmed).
What it is: the same CPI, but with petrol and diesel taken out, so you can see what is happening to everything else.
Why it matters: it shows that most of the jump above 3% is fuel. But 2.9% is still near the top of the band, so other prices are not exactly calm either.

rows.n: Average of the RBNZ’s core inflation measures
w: What it is: “core” measures strip out the jumpiest prices (like fuel) to show the underlying trend. The RBNZ looks at several (for example a trimmed mean, which drops the biggest rises and falls each quarter). We only collected their average, not each one.
Why it matters: the underlying trend rose from 2.4% to 2.7% in one quarter. It is still inside the band (the RBNZ says “all except one” core measure is), but moving the wrong way.
What it is: prices of things that cannot be shipped across borders, like rent, haircuts, insurance and council rates. They depend mostly on New Zealand’s own economy and wages.
Why it matters: this is the part of inflation the OCR can influence most. At 3.4% it is above the band, which tells the RBNZ that domestic price pressure has not fully cooled.
What it is: prices of things that are traded internationally or compete with imports, like petrol, cars, electronics and some food.
Why it matters: almost all of the 4.9% is fuel; without fuel it is 2.1%. That is the classic sign of an imported energy shock. A weaker Kiwi dollar can push this up further.

rows.n: Petrol and diesel prices (Selected price indexes)
rows.v: Petrol +17.9%, diesel +45.8% vs a year ago
w: What it is: Stats NZ now publishes monthly price indexes for some items between the quarterly CPI reports. Treasury summarised the August figures.
Why it matters: fuel is the main source of today’s inflation. Brent oil jumped again in late September and early October, so the September and December quarters may still see high fuel prices.

rows.v: +1.9% vs a year ago (+0.3% in the month)
w: What it is: the monthly change in prices at the supermarket and for takeaways. The yearly figure (1.9%) comes from Treasury’s summary.
Why it matters: food inflation has slowed from 4.5% in February to below 2%, and rents were flat in August. That is evidence fuel has not spread into everything.
What it is: the prices businesses get for what they produce, before it reaches shops.
Why it matters: a 1.6% rise in a single quarter is fast. Business costs often reach shop prices a few months later, which is why the RBNZ worries about “second-round” effects.

rows.n: Inflation expectations, 2 years ahead (RBNZ Survey of Expectations)
w: What it is: the RBNZ asks professional forecasters and business leaders what inflation they expect in two years’ time.
Why it matters: if people expect high inflation, they set prices and wages to match, and it becomes self-fulfilling. 2.3% is close to target and has fallen, which is reassuring.

missing: September quarter CPI: due before the Oct 28 decision (exact Stats NZ date not confirmed)
Individual core measures (trimmed mean, weighted median, sectoral factor model): only the average was collected
Household inflation expectations (numbers): not collected; the RBNZ says household one-year expectations “remained elevated”
Selected price indexes for September: due Oct 16

G.name: Jobs
G.intro: These numbers show whether New Zealanders can find work and how fast pay is rising. The RBNZ does not have a separate jobs target, but its law tells it to avoid unnecessary instability in employment, and spare workers (slack) keep wage and price growth in check.

w: What it is: the share of people who want a job and are actively looking but do not have one. New Zealand measures it once a quarter.
Why it matters: 5.6% shows a lot of spare capacity. The RBNZ forecasts it to stay above 5% until 2028, which is one reason some members worry more about growth than prices.
What it is: the number of people with jobs, from the same survey.
Why it matters: jobs are being added, but not fast enough to absorb new workers. The RBNZ: “Employment growth has not been sufficient to fully absorb new entrants into the labour market”.
What it is: a monthly count of jobs from tax records, which comes out faster than the quarterly survey.
Why it matters: yearly job growth turned from −1.9% in April to +0.9% in August (Treasury). Hiring is slowly picking up.
What it is: the share of adults who are working or looking for work.
Why it matters: a high share means plenty of people are available to work, which keeps wage pressure low.

rows.n: Labour cost index (salary and wage rates)
w: What it is: how fast pay rates for the same jobs are rising, ignoring promotions or job changes.
Why it matters: pay rising 2.0% while prices rise 4.1% means workers are losing buying power. For the RBNZ this is reassuring: wages are not feeding a price spiral.
What it is: average pay per hour across all jobs, from a survey of businesses.
Why it matters: it is slowing, and real (after-inflation) pay fell in the June quarter. That makes it less likely that wages keep inflation high.

rows.v: +5.3% in the month, +9.7% vs a year ago
w: What it is: a private count of job advertisements, reported by Treasury.
Why it matters: rising job ads usually come before rising employment. But with about 420 applicants per ad, competition for jobs is still fierce.

missing: September quarter labour market statistics: due early November, after the decision (exact date not confirmed)
Underutilisation rate and long-term unemployment numbers: not collected

G.name: Growth and spending
G.intro: These numbers show how fast New Zealand’s economy is growing and whether households are spending. Weak growth argues for a gentler brake; strong growth makes room for a higher OCR.

rows.v: +0.2% in the quarter (+1.7% vs a year ago)
w: What it is: GDP is the total value of everything the country produces. A 0.2% quarterly rise is slow but positive.
Why it matters: the RBNZ had expected about flat to 0.2%, so this was no surprise. It forecasts 0.5% for the September quarter. A weak economy makes raising rates riskier.
What it is: the after-inflation value of what households spent, from the expenditure measure of GDP.
Why it matters: households are cautious, squeezed by fuel costs, weak pay growth and falling house prices. This is the part of the economy the OCR hits hardest.
What it is: how much shops sold, after removing price changes.
Why it matters: falling volumes mean people are buying fewer things, even if they are paying more for them.
What it is: the value of goods sold overseas, like dairy, meat and fruit.
Why it matters: exporters are the bright spot. A cheap Kiwi dollar helps them. Governor Breman expects a “resilient export sector” to lead the recovery.
What it is: a private monthly survey asking firms whether they expect business conditions to improve (a positive net number means more optimists than pessimists).
Why it matters: firms remain optimistic despite fuel costs, which hints growth may pick up in the second half of the year.
What it is: an index of house sale prices from the Real Estate Institute of New Zealand, reported by Treasury. House sales were down 13% from a year earlier.
Why it matters: most New Zealand households hold their wealth in houses. Falling prices make people feel poorer and spend less. Higher mortgage rates add to the pressure.

rows.n: Real house prices (BIS index on FRED)
rows.s: Bank for International Settlements via FRED
w: What it is: house prices adjusted for inflation, compiled by the Bank for International Settlements.
Why it matters: it confirms the longer trend of slowly falling real house prices. It is several months out of date.
What it is: the difference between what New Zealand earns from the rest of the world and what it pays out. A deficit means it relies on overseas borrowing.
Why it matters: a wider deficit can weigh on the Kiwi dollar. Merchandise terms of trade fell 9.4% in a year, partly because imported fuel got dearer.

missing: September quarter GDP: due mid-December, after the decision (date not confirmed)
Building consents and the NZIER Quarterly Survey of Business Opinion (Q3): not collected

G.name: The rate and money markets
G.intro: The OCR is the RBNZ’s main lever. Market interest rates show what investors expect the RBNZ to do next, and they set the price of fixed-rate mortgages.

w: What it is: the interest rate banks earn on money they leave at the Reserve Bank, and close to what they pay to borrow from it. It flows through to floating mortgage rates and savings accounts.
Why it matters: it is the gas and brake pedal. It was cut to 2.25% in November 2025, then raised in July and September 2026.
What it is: the rate banks charge each other to borrow for three months.
Why it matters: it sits about 0.48 points above the OCR. Since three-month lending covers both the October and December decisions, this gap says markets expect the OCR to rise soon (our reading).
What it is: the interest rate the government pays to borrow for two years.
Why it matters: at more than a full point above the OCR, it shows investors expect several OCR rises over the next two years. Two-year fixed mortgages follow similar wholesale rates.
What it is: the interest rate the government pays to borrow for ten years.

Why it matters: it jumped about half a point since June, following global bond rates up. Treasury called 5.13% in late September a high. Higher long rates cool the economy without the RBNZ doing anything.

rows.n: Market odds of an October rise
w: What it is: Treasury’s reading of financial market pricing. Markets also priced the OCR at 3.75% by end-2027.
Why it matters: it is the only market-odds figure we found, and it is about four weeks old. Oil has risen further since then.

rows.v: Rising to about 3.2% over two years
w: What it is: the path for the OCR the RBNZ thinks fits its central forecast. It is a forecast, not a promise.
Why it matters: 3.2% implies roughly two more 0.25-point rises. The RBNZ also noted market pricing of about 3% by end-2026.
What it is: how many US dollars one New Zealand dollar buys.
Why it matters: a weaker Kiwi dollar makes imports like fuel, cars and electronics dearer in NZ dollars, adding to inflation.
What it is: the Kiwi dollar measured against a basket of 17 trading partners’ currencies.
Why it matters: the RBNZ’s September forecasts assumed 66.9. Today’s 63.94 is about 4% weaker, which, other things equal, means more imported inflation than the RBNZ planned for (our calculation).

missing: 2-year swap rate (exact level): not collected; Treasury said it rose above 4.0% in mid-September
Bank mortgage rates on offer: not collected (the RBNZ said 6-month to 2-year rates rose 0.20–0.30 points after May)

G.name: What the RBNZ said
G.intro: What the Reserve Bank and its Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) have said, in their own words. Quotes are verbatim from the linked pages.

w: What it said: “Conditional on the central economic outlook, members judged that the OCR may need to increase further.” The decision was by consensus.
Why it matters: the RBNZ is openly signalling more rises, but uses the softer word “may”.

What it said: Gourley, Silk, Gai and Breman saw inflation risks to the upside; Conway and Hansen saw them as balanced, with downside risks to activity. All agreed downside activity risks were significant.
Why it matters: in July only two members (Gai, Gourley) saw upside risk. The Committee has moved toward worrying more about inflation.
What it said: “while further OCR increases appear likely at upcoming meetings, their timing is highly uncertain.”
Why it matters: this line framed the September rise. October is the next “upcoming meeting”.
What it said: Breman, Silk and Conway voted to hold; Hansen, Gourley and Gai voted to raise to 2.50%. The Chair’s casting vote decided it.
Why it matters: it shows how divided the Committee can be. Votes have been named since May 2026 when a vote is taken.

rows.v: Oil and long rates a challenge
w: What it said: “If higher oil prices persist, they are expected to result in somewhat higher near-term inflation” and “As always, we will assess incoming data and global developments ahead of our next decision in October”.
Why it matters: it is the latest on-the-record comment we found. It flags oil as the key risk but does not pre-commit.
What it said: “businesses pass on cost increases more readily now than in the past” and “anchored inflation expectations cannot be taken for granted”.
Why it matters: it explains why the RBNZ does not simply ignore a fuel shock, even though Conway was one of the members seeing balanced risks in September.
What it said: Senior Manager Economics Rebecca Williams joins the Committee as an internal member from October 15, 2026 for one year. Assistant Governor Karen Silk leaves the Bank in mid-December.
Why it matters: the October decision will likely be made by seven members, not six (our reading), so a 3–3 split like May’s is less likely.

missing: Record of the October meeting: published with the decision on Oct 28
Full September media-conference transcript: not read

G.name: Global conditions
G.intro: New Zealand imports all its crude oil and fuel and sells much of what it makes overseas, so world energy prices and other central banks matter a lot.

w: What it is: the world benchmark price of crude oil, in US dollars.

Why it matters: the RBNZ’s September forecasts assumed Dubai oil of about US$85 a barrel for the September quarter. Oil is now far above that, so fuel inflation may last longer than the RBNZ expected.
What it is: the US benchmark oil price.
Why it matters: it is also near US$100, confirming that energy remains expensive worldwide.
What it is: the oil price the RBNZ built into its September forecasts.
Why it matters: comparing it with today’s prices is the simplest way to see that inflation risks have grown since the last decision.

rows.n: US Federal Reserve rate (top of range)
w: What it is: the top of the US central bank’s target range.
Why it matters: higher US rates pull money toward the US dollar and weaken the Kiwi. The Fed decides on Oct 28 US time, which is after the RBNZ in New Zealand time.
What it is: the European Central Bank’s main policy rate.
Why it matters: major central banks are raising rates into the energy shock, which supports the case for the RBNZ to keep going too.
What it is: how many Australian dollars one Kiwi dollar buys. Australia is New Zealand’s biggest trading partner after China.
Why it matters: a weaker Kiwi against the Aussie makes Australian goods dearer and New Zealand holidays cheaper for Australians.
What it is: the OECD’s projection for global growth, as summarised by Treasury.
Why it matters: steady world growth supports demand for New Zealand exports. The OECD also raised its G20 inflation forecast to 4.1% for 2026.

missing: Dubai crude price (the RBNZ’s benchmark): not collected
China and Australia activity data: not collected
Global dairy prices (GDT auctions): not collected
